lesson.title: Scientific notation
lesson.body:
Split every number into mantissa × power of ten and handle the two parts separately:

  • Multiply: multiply the mantissas, add the exponents.
  • Divide: divide the mantissas, subtract the exponents.
  • Renormalize: if the mantissa lands outside 1–10, shift one place and fix the exponent (42 × 102 = 4.2 × 103; 0.286 × 1011 = 2.86 × 1010).

Example: (6 × 105) × (7 × 10−3): 6 × 7 = 42, 5 + (−3) = 2 → 42 × 102 = 4.2 × 103.

Example: (3.7 × 108) ÷ (6.2 × 10−4): 3.7 ÷ 6.2 ≈ 0.6 (check 6.2 × 0.6 = 3.72), so ≈ 0.597; 8 − (−4) = 12 → 5.97 × 1011.

Tips: say the exponent bookkeeping out loud — sign errors with negative exponents are the #1 mistake. Use your reciprocal anchors for division (÷ 8 = × 0.125, ÷ 7 ≈ × 0.143). For chains, do all the exponents in one pass at the end. Type answers as e.g. 5.97e11.

lesson.title: Fast estimation
lesson.body:
Goal: a few-percent answer in seconds. Three habits:

  • Round to friendly numbers — balanced. Friendly mantissas: 1, 1.2, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7.5, 8, 9. In a product, round one factor up and another down; in a quotient, round top and bottom the same way.
  • Track the exponent separately. Write each number as mantissa × 10n, multiply the small mantissas, add up the exponents at the end.
  • Quantify the rounding. Each rounding changes the result by about its own percentage (÷ flips the sign). Add them up and correct: small errors add, to first order.

Example: 347 × 58 ≈ 350 × 60 = 21 000. Errors: +0.9% and +3.4% → ≈ 4.3% high → 21 000 − 4.3% ≈ 20 100 (true 20 126).

Example: 347 × 0.0219 × 58 ÷ 7.3: 3.5 × 2 × 6 ÷ 7 = 6, exponents 2 − 2 + 1 − 0 = 1 → 60. Errors +0.9%, −8.7%, +3.4%, ÷ 7.3→7 +4.3% → net ≈ 0 → ≈ 60 (true 60.4).

Roots and powers: make the exponent even, then √M ≈ a + (M − a²)/(2a) using the nearest whole or half square ((n + ½)² = n(n+1) + ¼, e.g. 6.5² = 42.25): √(4.2 × 107) = √42 × 103 ≈ 6.48 × 103. Squares: 3 600² = 3.6² × 106 = 12.96 × 106.

lesson.title: Reciprocals
lesson.body:
Every reciprocal comes from your memorized 1/2 … 1/16 by one of two moves.

1. Factor. If x splits into two anchors, divide one reciprocal by the other factor: 1/24 = 1/12 ÷ 2 = 0.0833 ÷ 2 = 0.0417; 1/42 = 1/7 ÷ 6 = 0.143 ÷ 6 = 0.0238; 1/70 = 1/7 ÷ 10 = 0.0143.

2. Anchor + correction. Otherwise pick the nearest "nice" number a and use

  1/(a + d) ≈ (1/a)·(1 − d/a)

— a number bigger than the anchor has a slightly smaller reciprocal, by the same percentage. The error is only (d/a)², so with d/a ≈ 3% you're good to 0.1%.
1/37: anchor 36 = 4 × 9, 1/36 = 0.111 ÷ 4 = 0.0278; 37 is 1/36 ≈ 2.8% bigger → 0.0278 − 0.0008 = 0.0270 (true 0.02703).
1/59: 1/60 = 0.01667, 59 is 1/60 smaller → 0.01667 + 0.00028 = 0.01695.

Decimals and exponents: slide the decimal point first, then do a 2-digit reciprocal: 1/0.0042 = 104/42 ≈ 0.0238 × 104 = 238; 1/(3.7 × 105) = (1/37) × 10−4 ≈ 2.70 × 10−6.
